issues.item: Tactile (Restrained): Feeling physically restrained or held down
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'feeling physically restrained or held down' implies a hands-on assault/restraint context that is not supported by the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and appraisal items consistently describe ongoing danger/hypervigilance related to being followed or encountered, making this tactile restraint trigger clinically discordant with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically to stop thinking about the event is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The formulation and items emphasize hypervigilance, danger appraisals, and place/proximity avoidance, but there are no memory/intrusion items or other indicators of overwhelming internal re-experiencing that would make this strategy fit coherently here. It reads as a symptom-management strategy for a different presentation than the one otherwise described.

'Drug Use' is the only clearly incoherent item in the selected five components. The rest of the profile forms a coherent stalking-related pattern: triggers of proximity/being followed/bicycle plausibly cue threat; threat items reflect hypervigilance and false alarms; negative appraisals center on danger, distrust, and lack of justice; and checking surroundings/avoiding location plausibly follow from those appraisals and threat beliefs. In contrast, drug use is not supported by the rest of the selected content: there are no accompanying items indicating broader emotion-regulation coping, dissociative distress, sleep-related self-medication, or generalized avoidance that would make substance use a clinically grounded strategy here. Given the formulation, Maladaptive Strategies is strongly linked from Threat and moderately from Negative Appraisals, so selected strategies should plausibly arise from the expressed threat beliefs/appraisals. 'Drug Use' feels disconnected from the otherwise specific hypervigilant stalking profile and is the only item that clinicians would be likely to question as belonging to the same coherent self-report pattern.

vignette: Anaïs had always loved her daily commute to work on her bicycle, feeling the wind in her hair and the sun on her face. But that all changed about a year ago, when she started noticing a familiar face lurking around every corner. At first, she thought it was just coincidence, but as the days went by, she became convinced that someone was stalking her. It started with small things - finding strange gifts on her doorstep, receiving mysterious phone calls in the dead of night. But soon, the stalker's behavior escalated to following her everywhere she went. Anaïs would see him lurking outside her office building, or riding a bike behind her as she cycled home. She felt like she was constantly looking over her shoulder, never knowing when he would appear next. The experience left Anaïs shaken and on edge. Even now, months after the stalking finally stopped, she can't shake the feeling of being watched. She's become hyper-vigilant, constantly scanning her surroundings for signs of threat. She'll often find herself checking the street outside her office window, or peering over her shoulder as she walks down the street. Anaïs has started to avoid certain locations altogether - particularly the route she used to take on her daily commute. She's too afraid that she'll see him again, and can't bear the thought of being followed once more. Instead, she takes a longer route to work, one that avoids the areas where she knows he used to lurk. She's also developed a habit of sitting near exits whenever she's in a public place. She feels safer knowing that she can make a quick escape if needed. And even though it's been months since the stalking stopped, Anaïs still finds herself planning escape routes wherever she goes - identifying the nearest door or window, just in case. Anaïs' fears have also started to seep into other areas of her life. She's become more jumpy and easily startled, often reacting as if she's in danger even when there's no real threat present. Her friends and family have noticed a change in her too - she's become more withdrawn and anxious, always on the lookout for potential dangers. Despite her best efforts to move on, Anaïs can't shake the feeling that the world is a fundamentally unsafe place. She's angry that her stalker was never caught or brought to justice, and feels like no one took her concerns seriously at the time. As a result, she's started to distrust others - wondering if they might be hiding something beneath their friendly facades. Anaïs' job as a graphic designer has also suffered as a result of her experiences. She used to love working on creative projects, but now finds it hard to focus on anything except the potential dangers lurking outside her window. Her relationships with her colleagues have become strained too - they don't understand why she's always so jumpy and anxious. It was only when Anaïs' husband sat her down and told her that he couldn't take it anymore - that he felt like he was losing his wife to anxiety and fear - that Anaïs realized she needed help. She's hoping that therapy will be able to help her rebuild her sense of safety, and learn to trust others again. But for now, she's still trapped in a world of constant threat, always on the lookout for potential dangers lurking around every corner.
